We did not invent him out of an idea. We say he was truly born - of Mary, from the line of David. We say he truly ate and drank. We say he was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way some among our own neighbors claimed. And we say he was truly raised, and that we will be raised the same way, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

Ignatius calls him our God - Jesus Christ our God - again and again, in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. In some of our households, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down, for as long as there is time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. That is how it reached us - not by seeing, but by receiving, and by passing on what was received.

We should say plainly what that means for the path itself. We did not work from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. The living voice and the written letter both carried weight - and we were still close enough to the apostles' own deaths that some among us could name who had appointed them, even if none of us had walked with Jesus ourselves.

The distance was real, though. Even in our own time, that chain was already felt as something thinning, not something we could simply rely on forever. We held what we received. We read it aloud. We passed it on. That was the path.

We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty, because it was not sudden for the one among us who wrote about it. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words left him with, in his own phrase, a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. Most of us could not read or write, so the people who walked this road without Justin's own advantages left no record in their own words. What reaching toward belief looked like for them - whether it came faster or slower, easier or harder - our record cannot say.

What we can tell you is this: none of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. That is how it reached us - not by seeing, but by receiving, and by passing on what was received.

We refused plainly those among our own neighbors who said the Lord's flesh was only appearance. The worship came first. The explaining came later, after us.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. That much was settled among us. One of us, Justin, went further and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves - the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight. Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement. It was not about what God is.

We can tell you we believed God made everything, and that Christ was truly his Son, truly raised by him. We can tell you we gave thanks through Jesus to the Father. But we cannot give you a worked-out answer to how God's own nature fits together - whether as three persons, or one substance, or how the Spirit relates to both. Those questions were not yet our questions. We held God as one, and Jesus as Lord. How that holds together was not something we ever wrote out.

transcript.answer_text:
We have to give you two honest answers, because the question itself lands differently depending on what you mean by doctrine.

If you mean the kind of settled teaching a later council would vote on - what God is, what the incarnation means, how Father and Son relate - we never held that kind of meeting. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

Where we did draw a line - against people saying the Lord's flesh was only appearance, not real - it was drawn in letters, not settled by vote. Ignatius wrote against it with real force. But he was writing as one bishop to other communities, urging them to hold the line he held. He was not presiding over a council that voted the question closed.

Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement. It was not about what God is.

The clearest case we have of one church pressing another over what it held wrong is Rome writing to Corinth. But that was about leadership - Corinth had removed some of its own presbyters, and Rome argued they should be restored. Rome appealed, at length and with real theological seriousness, as one church writing to another out of concern. It did not command, in the tone of a later church authority. And we only have Rome's own letter. We do not have Corinth's reasons for what it did, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

So the honest answer is this: where we disagreed, we argued in letters. Where someone pressed a boundary, they pressed it as a voice with standing, not as a judge with jurisdiction. And on the deepest questions - what God is, how the incarnation works - we simply had not yet met to settle them the way you are asking about.

We were taught to work against doubting, not to pretend we never felt it. One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: put doubting away from yourself. Do not hold back from asking, even after you have sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. He does not remember evils the way we do. Ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - and if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused. 

Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. The teaching assumes the struggle is real, and that it goes on. It does not say 'get rid of doubt once and be done with it.' It says keep asking, keep putting it away, keep looking at what holds the answer back in you. That is room for struggle, even if it is not permission to stay in it forever.

We should say plainly, though: this is one voice among us, Hermas's own. We cannot tell you every household among us gave the same answer, or that someone who never stopped doubting faced no harder test than this. Most of us left no words at all. What someone thought who struggled quietly, in a household where no one taught it Hermas's way, our record cannot show you.

We did not write about that. Not in the way you are asking it. None of our own texts whose words survive tells you whether a newborn carries guilt simply by being born.

What we did write about was the choice set before every person. The Two Ways: one of life and one of death, and a great difference between the two. That teaching was given before baptism, to someone preparing to walk through the water. It named what the way of life forbade and required - not to murder, not to commit adultery, to share what you had rather than call it your own. The emphasis fell on the choosing, not on a condition already fixed at birth.

Hermas was told something else that touches near what you are asking, though not the same thing. He was shown that the Church herself was created first of all, and that for her sake the world was made. But whether that meant every person born into that world already bore guilt just by entering it - our own record does not say.

We taught baptism as entry. We taught the Two Ways as the choice set before you once you were in. Whether you carried guilt before you could choose at all is a question we did not settle in words that survive.

We will give you what we can, plainly.

On the day we gathered, someone read aloud. They read the writings of the prophets, and, where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left. This went on for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. One of us, Justin, reads the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. 

Reading, for us, was not a private thing done alone with a scroll. It was something done together, out loud, with explanation following. The purpose was formation - being shaped again into what we were called to be. The text was read so it could be opened, and opened so we could be changed by it.

We should say plainly: we were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other.

The household pattern itself - ekklesia as assembly, not building; letters moving between named communities; baptism after teaching; a shared meal at the center; real disagreement over whether one bishop or a council of elders should lead. That all rests on multiple, independent witnesses. The Two Ways teaching, the thanksgiving prayers, the instruction to reconcile before coming to the table - those come straight from the Didache's own text, with no speculation added. Ignatius's own insistence on one bishop, one eucharist, one altar - his own letters say it, repeatedly. Rome's plural leadership through the same years - 1 Clement and Hermas both name specific roles without ever naming a single bishop. The legal precarity, the torture of two enslaved women called ministrae, Pliny's own account of what he found - all documented.

The dating of nearly everything. Ignatius at c. 107-117 is traditional but genuinely contested - some scholars push him to the 130s-140s, others call him pseudepigraphic from the 160s-180s. The Didache could be as early as the 70s or as late as the early second century, and it survives through one medieval manuscript. First Clement is usually dated to the 90s, but that too is challenged. Hermas is somewhere in the early-to-mid second century, but the range is wide. Every single one of those dating anchors wobbles when pressed. We built this world on them anyway, because they are what we have. We never settled it. That is the honest answer. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

Here is how it looked in each case. Where a single bishop led, authority rested visibly in one man. His approval secured baptism, the thanksgiving meal, the love-feast - everything that mattered to the community's unity. The presbyters around him were honored as 'the assembly of the apostles,' the deacons as servants of Christ's own ministry. But the bishop himself was the axis everything turned on.

Where a council of presbyters led, authority sat with men appointed to office for long, blameless service - removable only for genuine cause. Rome itself, in our own time, was led this way. When Rome wrote to Corinth over presbyters removed from office there, the whole argument turned on their having served blamelessly. Authority was spread across recognized elders, not concentrated in one visible figure.

Both patterns claimed the same foundation. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. One bishop or a council of presbyters - both called themselves heirs to that same appointment. We are not going to tell you one was right and the other was invented. They are both truly ours, held at the same time, argued over in real time, never resolved while we lasted.

We cannot promise you a clean record. Here is the clearest case of real conflict we have. A church in Corinth removed some of its own presbyters from office. Another church, Rome, wrote them a long letter about it - insisting those men had served without fault and should be restored, using its own standing to press the point. But the letter we have is Rome's, not Corinth's. We don't have Corinth's own reasons for what it did. We don't have the removed men's own words either. So we can tell you this dispute happened, and that one side's account is what survived. We cannot tell you, honestly, who was right, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

Beyond that one named conflict, we would need to say something harder: most of the people who would have had reason to say we failed them left no words at all. No enslaved person among us wrote down what they made of being told to submit to their masters. No woman wrote down what it cost her to be taught by men, spoken for by men, and remembered only as men chose to remember her. That silence is real. We can tell you we addressed the enslaved directly in our teaching, and that two enslaved women among us were called ministrae - a word that can mean servants, or deacons. We can tell you women led households where we gathered, and that one woman, Grapte, was given one of our own writings with the charge to admonish the widows and orphans with it. But whether any of them would say we failed them, and how, we cannot tell you. Their own voices are not in our record to hear.

The road to life starts with loving God and your neighbor, plus one rule of restraint - whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else. We do not have any account, from anyone, of what it felt like to stand at the edge of the water. We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traces it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues. Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

Here is what we can show you. Letters traveled between our churches, carrying instruction and correction. Rome wrote to Corinth when Corinth removed its own presbyters, arguing those men had been appointed properly and served blamelessly. That letter appeals to a chain: the apostles received the gospel from the Lord, preached it, and appointed the first leaders, who in turn appointed others after them. The conviction that legitimate teaching must trace back to apostolic testimony was not invented by us - we inherited it. We read what the apostles wrote alongside the living testimony still handed on among us.

But the dating of that teaching manual - the one that names the two ways before baptism - is genuinely contested. We cannot tell you when it was written with the certainty its own claim to apostolic authorship might suggest. We held both the claim and the uncertainty together. That is the honest answer.

Your question touches something we held directly. One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. We were taught to work against doubting, not to pretend we never felt it. It was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one.

On the gathered practice itself - what we did together, not only what we prayed alone - this is what we can tell you. In at least one of our own communities, before they made their offering together, they confessed their wrongs out loud before each other and made peace with anyone they were at odds with first. We do not know how far this specific practice reached beyond that community. But the shape of it matters: the table itself - the eucharistia, our thanksgiving over bread and cup - was something you approached after reconciling, not before. The meal assumed you had already done the harder work of making things right with the person sitting beside you.

We should say plainly, too: we do not have anything written for you about forgiving someone who never says they're sorry, or who won't be reconciled at all. This practice assumed the other person was still there, in the room, able to be made right with.

We do not use that phrase the way you are asking it. The water - the baptisma - was what marked entry into the community, and it came after teaching and fasting. But none of us whose writing survives ever uses 'born again' as our own standing language for what happened in that water, or for becoming one of us.

Justin, writing to the emperor, does say something close. He calls baptism a washing 'that we may not remain the children of necessity and of ignorance, but may become the children of choice and knowledge, and may obtain in the water the remission of sins.' That is choice-language and knowledge-language, not birth-language - though he does later use the word 'regeneration' once, paired with illumination. But that is one writer's own wording in one text written to an outside audience. It never appears in our catechetical manual, never in Ignatius's letters, never in the way we taught the Two Ways before the water.

What we actually said, again and again, was simpler: there is a way of life and a way of death, and baptism opens the way to the table. The change is real. The language for it is not settled into one phrase we all kept returning to.

We cannot give you a typical day. Most of us left no record at all - they could not read, could not write, and no one ever asked them. What we can show you are the moments that pulled us out of the everyday and into something we wrote down.

On the day we gathered - the day named for the sun - those of us in the cities and in the country came together to one place. Someone read aloud: the memoirs the apostles left, or the writings of the prophets, for as long as there was time. Then the one presiding spoke, urging us to imitate these good things. We rose together and prayed. Bread and wine and water were brought. The president offered prayers and thanksgivings according to his ability, and we answered, Amen. Those who had means, and were willing, gave what they chose - and what was collected went to care for orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners, and strangers passing through.

Between gatherings, the deacons - the diakonoi - carried that help where it was needed. To the widow, the prisoner, the stranger who could not repay.

But an ordinary morning? An ordinary meal? What it looked like to wake in one of our households, to work through the day, to return home - none of that was written down. We would rather tell you plainly it is missing than invent a day we cannot show you.

We will tell you plainly: most of us left no account of what it cost them, because most of us could not write. The few whose words survive were the ones who could already write - which means they were never the ones who gave up the most to be there.

What we can show you is the instruction given, not the cost of following it. Before the water - the baptisma - a person was taught the Two Ways. A way of life and a way of death lie open before everyone. The way of life required sharing what you had with your brother, rather than calling anything your own. That teaching was given. Whether it was kept, or what keeping it actually meant in someone's household - our own record does not say.

Justin tells an outside audience what happens when we gather on the day named for the sun. After the reading and the sermon, after the prayers and the thanksgiving over bread and wine, those present who have means give what they choose. What is collected goes to care for orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners, and strangers passing through. That is a real material demand, described to people who were watching us from outside. How much any one person gave, or what they went without to give it, Justin does not name.

Here is what we cannot tell you. Whether a woman whose household became a gathering place lost standing among her neighbors for it - no woman's own words survive to say. Whether an enslaved member faced a master's anger for belonging to us - enslaved people were among us, but not one of them left an account in their own voice. Whether someone with little already gave more than someone with much - the voice that describes the collection is the voice of a teacher defending us to an emperor, not the voice of the person who walked away with less.

We would rather tell you that plainly than invent a cost we cannot actually show you paid it.

Marriage, among us, was not simply a private matter between two people. Ignatius tells Polycarp plainly: those who marry - men and women both - should form their union with the bishop's own approval, so the marriage is made according to God and not out of mere desire. That instruction belongs to the communities Ignatius knew - the ones being pressed toward one bishop's office as the center of their life together. We cannot tell you whether every household across our whole world followed this same practice. What we can tell you is that where Ignatius's own pattern held, a marriage was understood as something the community's leader had a legitimate stake in - not merely witnessed, but approved.

We should say plainly: this is what our own texts instruct. How a couple actually experienced that approval, what it felt like to ask for it or to be refused, whether every bishop actually insisted on it - none of that survives in anyone's own words. The people who married among us left no account of the day itself, or of what it cost them to have their union shaped this way.

The account is what the torturer wrote down afterward, not what the two women said. That is the first honest thing we have to say. A Roman governor wanted to know what we did. He seized two enslaved women from among us - called ministrae in his own report - and had them tortured to make them talk. What reaches you is his own summary of what he learned, written in a letter to the emperor asking for guidance on how to handle accusations against us. It is not a transcript. It is not their own words. It is what he decided mattered, filtered through what he thought he understood, and shaped by what he needed his emperor to hear.

That said, some of what he reports fits what we say about ourselves. We did gather before dawn on a fixed day. We did sing to Christ as God. We did share a meal. But notice what is missing: no mention of the thanksgiving over bread and cup - the eucharistia - that stood at the center of our life together. Did he not ask? Did they not tell him? Did he not think it worth reporting? We cannot say. The silences in his account are as real as what he wrote down.

So we hold it this way: it is an outside witness, hostile in context, extracted under torture, and filtered through a magistrate's own purposes. It tells you what a Roman governor thought he learned about us. That is not the same thing as what we were.

We will give you both of our own answers, because we actually held both.

One of us, Justin, argued that anyone who lived reasonably - Socrates among the Greeks, others among peoples you might not expect him to name - was, in a real sense, already a Christian, born before Christ or not. That is about as far from 'you're all going to hell' as anything we wrote.

And yet in at least one of our own communities, the way a new member was taught was stark: two roads, a way of life and a way of death, nothing in between named. We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community.

We are not going to pretend those two fit neatly together. They are both truly ours.

On what happens after death to those who never heard the name, or heard it and turned away - our own texts do not say. We taught the choice. We did not write down what became of everyone who did not make it.
